name: Wendy Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We grow vegetables on contract for a supermarket chain: little gem lettuce, broccoli, leeks and spring onions on about ninety hectares. In season I'm up at half four, and by five I'm checking the overnight order from the supermarket on my phone, because what they want changes every day and whatever they don't take goes to waste. Then I'm out with the harvest crew, about twenty-five people in summer, and my husband Kevin runs the packing shed. What I love is a perfect field of broccoli heads all ready on the same morning. What wears me out is the supermarket buyer changing the order at eleven at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you keep up with orders that change that fast?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use an AI assistant every day, honestly it's like a second manager. It looks at the supermarket's forecasts, the weather and what's in the field, and tells me what to cut tomorrow and what to plant next week. Two years ago we also trialled a weeding robot in the leeks, it was slow, but it worked, and I've been saving towards one since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's a great tool, use it. I'm the one at the growers' meetings telling everyone to try it, and some of them think I've gone soft in the head. I'd say we've got to keep up, because the supermarkets certainly will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's business as usual, and that's fine. The assistant already saves me a couple of hours a day, and a better one would save a bit more. What really decides my year is the supermarket contract and the weather, and AI doesn't change who holds the power there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep putting money aside for the weeding robot, about eight hundred a month. I'd use the assistant to plan the planting calendar for next season and to check the supermarket's contract terms, which are written to confuse you. And I'd start training Ali, my crew foreman, to use it on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit impatient for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why train Ali, rather than just doing it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm fifty-eight and I won't be here forever, and Ali's the best foreman I've had in twenty years. He came to us at nineteen and worked his way up. If he can run the planning, he can run this farm one day, or a bigger one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the contract terms are written to confuse you. What does the assistant catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little things that cost a lot, like who pays if a lorry's late or what happens to a crop they cancel at a day's notice. Last year it spotted a clause that would have made us pay for their rejected loads. I'd never have seen it at midnight.

S0.say: It's a great tool, so use it, even if some at the growers' meetings think I've gone soft in the head. We've got to keep up, because the supermarkets certainly will.
S0.think: For me it's business as usual, with an assistant that already saves a couple of hours a day. What really decides my year is the supermarket contract and the weather, and AI doesn't change who holds the power.
S0.do: Keeps saving about eight hundred a month toward a weeding robot and uses the assistant to plan next season and check contract terms. Starts training her crew foreman Ali to use the tool on his phone.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little impatient for more.
S0.quote: Last year it spotted a clause that would have made us pay for their rejected loads. I'd never have seen it at midnight.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy uses AI as a second manager to cope with a demanding supermarket contract. She is already saving for robots and thinking about succession through her foreman Ali, who worked his way up from nineteen. Her traditional values show in praising hard work and earned promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, slow is easier to plan for. But firms not hiring young people is short-sighted, because they'll run out of managers in ten years. I'd tell the growers' meeting we should take on more apprentices ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly good news. I get the tools steadily without anyone else jumping ahead. The worry is my son Michael, he's an IT support person at a firm in the city, and that's exactly the kind of beginner-level job that thins out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on two apprentices from the agricultural college, one for the field and one for the packing shed, so they learn the trade properly. That's about twelve thousand a year, which I'd find by cutting back on contract labour. And I'd keep pushing on the weeding robot, maybe buy one in the second or third year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit uneasy for Michael.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for apprentices by cutting contract labour. Who loses out there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency workers, a few of them, and I don't pretend that's nothing. But an apprentice gets a skill and stays, an agency worker comes for three weeks and goes. I'd rather build something than rent it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Michael?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get closer to the people side of IT, the managing, the dealing with customers. And I'd say, you know there's always a job here if you want one, though he'd rather be in an office. He hated weeding as a boy.

S1.say: Slow is easier to plan for, but firms not hiring young people are short-sighted and will run out of managers in ten years. Growers should take on more apprentices ourselves.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good news, with tools arriving steadily. The worry is my son Michael, whose IT support job in the city is exactly the beginner-level work that thins out.
S1.do: Takes on two college apprentices, one in the field and one in the packing shed, for about twelve thousand a year by cutting agency labour. Keeps planning to buy a weeding robot in the second or third year.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, a little uneasy for Michael.
S1.quote: I'd rather build something than rent it.
S1.fieldNote: She swaps agency workers for apprentices and is honest that some people lose out. Her traditional preference for learning a trade drives the choice. She sees her son's IT job as exposed and nudges him toward the people side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should keep out of it and let businesses adapt, but businesses should look after their own people, retrain them, not just dump them. Help should come from work, not cheques. And I'd say farming's hiring, come and learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for my farm and bad for my family. The assistants would make the planning even easier, and the supermarket's own office staff would shrink, so maybe fewer silly orders at eleven at night. But Michael's IT job and my daughter-in-law's admin job are both routine office work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite Michael to come and run the farm's systems, the assistants, the order tracking, the weeding robot when it comes. I'd pay him what he earns now, about thirty thousand, which would be a stretch. And I'd go ahead with the weeding robot in the spring rather than waiting, because labour would get more expensive as everyone wanted outdoor work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Michael, excited for the farm. The two don't sit easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said labour would get more expensive. Wouldn't it get cheaper with office people looking for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You'd think so, but office people don't last a week cutting lettuce in the rain, I've seen it. The ones who stay want proper wages and they're right to. So yes, more people, but not more of the right people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thirty thousand for Michael would be a stretch. How would you find it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the robot savings, partly, and from Kevin and me taking less. We've got about four months of costs in the bank. It would be tight, but that's what family businesses are for.

S2.say: The government should keep out and let businesses adapt, but businesses should retrain their own people rather than dump them. Help should come from work, not cheques, and farming's hiring.
S2.think: It's good for my farm and bad for my family, because planning gets easier and the supermarket's office may stop sending silly late-night orders. But Michael's IT job and my daughter-in-law's admin job are both routine office work.
S2.do: Invites Michael to run the farm's systems at about thirty thousand a year, funded partly from robot savings and partly by Wendy and Kevin taking less. Brings the weeding robot purchase forward to the spring, expecting good labour to get dearer.
S2.feel: Anxious for her son and excited for the farm, two feelings that don't sit easily together.
S2.quote: Office people don't last a week cutting lettuce in the rain, I've seen it.
S2.fieldNote: She sees a surprising effect: more job seekers but not more of the right people, so labour may get dearer. She plans to bring her son into the business at a real cost to the household. The split between her farm's gain and her family's risk is something she names herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who built these companies earned their money, but they owe something to the country that educated their workers. Not handouts, apprenticeships and investment in towns. I'd say the crisis is a sign we stopped valuing practical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do quite well. The supermarkets would still need vegetables, and if office workers lost jobs, people would cook at home more, so demand might even rise. Land prices up means my land's worth more. But I'd see a lot of anger, and I'd be careful not to look like I'm gloating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the weeding robot straight away and a second one in the autumn, and start looking at a harvest robot for the lettuce. I'd take on more people to run them, Ali and Michael at the front. And I'd give some of my crew a pay rise, because they'd be worth more to me and to everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Some guilt about doing well. And excited, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be careful not to look like you're gloating. What would that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not buying a new car, for one, the neighbours notice. Sponsoring the village football team again, which Kevin keeps saying we should. Keeping our heads down and our gate open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency workers I stopped using, if they don't find anything. And Kevin's brother, who's a solicitor's clerk and has never done a day's outdoor work. I'd offer him a job in the packing shed, and he'd hate it, but it'd be a wage.

S3.say: People who built these companies earned their money, but they owe something to the country that educated their workers, through apprenticeships and investment, not handouts. The crisis shows we stopped valuing practical work.
S3.think: I'd do quite well, because supermarkets still need vegetables and people cooking at home might push demand up, while my land is worth more. But there'd be a lot of anger, and I'd be careful not to look like I'm gloating.
S3.do: Buys the weeding robot immediately and a second in the autumn, and starts looking at a lettuce harvest robot with Ali and Michael running them. Gives some crew a pay rise and offers Kevin's brother packing shed work.
S3.feel: Mostly calm and openly excited, with some guilt about doing well.
S3.quote: Keeping our heads down and our gate open.
S3.fieldNote: Wendy is a likely winner here and says so, with some guilt. Her plans move fast into robots, but she shares gains through pay rises and jobs for relatives. She is careful about how success looks to neighbours, a sign of her strong community sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, robots are coming, so let's make sure our farmers own them, not just the big companies. I'd want the government out of the way on rules, but I'd want them to help with apprenticeships so people can learn to run the machines. I'd say that at the growers' meeting and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm torn. I'd be the first one on this road with a harvesting robot, and I'd still be in the field at five, because a supermarket contract doesn't care whose fault it was. But twenty-five people work my harvest, and most of them would be gone within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd lease a harvest robot rather than buy, because they'd get cheaper fast and I can't afford to be stuck with the wrong one. I'd keep Ali and train him to manage the machines, and I'd try to keep half the crew on the jobs robots can't do yet, like the packing shed and the fiddly crops. I'd tell the rest early, at the start of the season, not the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the machines, sad about the crew, worried about the money. All at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell the crew at the start of the season. What would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I'll keep as many of you as I can, and I'll give a reference to every one of you. I'd say it in the yard, all together, not in a letter. Some of them have worked for me for fifteen summers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want the government out of the way, but help with apprenticeships. Isn't that asking for both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably is, I'll give you that. I want them to stay out of telling me how to farm, and help with teaching people a trade. That doesn't feel like a contradiction to me, but I can see how it sounds.

S4.say: Robots are coming, so let's make sure our farmers own them, not just the big companies. Keep the government out of the way on rules, but have it help with apprenticeships so people learn to run the machines.
S4.think: I'm torn: I'd be the first on this road with a harvesting robot, and still in the field at five. But twenty-five people work my harvest, and most would be gone within three years.
S4.do: Leases a harvest robot rather than buying, expecting prices to fall fast, and trains Ali to manage the machines. Keeps about half the crew on packing and fiddly crops and tells the rest in the yard at the start of the season, with a reference for each.
S4.feel: Anxious, with excitement, sadness and money worries all at once.
S4.quote: Some of them have worked for me for fifteen summers.
S4.fieldNote: She would move first on robots but feels the cost to her crew sharply and plans to tell them face to face, early. When challenged on wanting government both out and in, she admits it sounds like a contradiction but holds her position. Her succession hopes rest on her foreman Ali running the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because of the crew. What would help is government support for apprenticeships so my people can learn to run the machines, and fair contracts from the supermarkets so small growers can afford them. And staying out of the way on everything else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the supermarkets. People think the robots are the big power, but it's the buyer with the order book. I'd be the first one on this road with a harvesting robot, and I'd still be in the field at five. A supermarket contract doesn't care whose fault it was.

headlineQuote: I'd be the first one on this road with a harvesting robot, and I'd still be in the field at five.
portrait: Wendy Zhang is a 58-year-old vegetable grower with about ninety hectares on supermarket contract, a husband who runs the packing shed, and a crew foreman she hopes will one day run the farm. She uses AI every day as a second manager, has been saving for a weeding robot, and likes learning a trade more than government help. Through the scenarios she sees her farm gaining while her son's IT job is at risk, and she brings him into the business at real cost. When robots arrive, she would lease one early but grieves for a harvest crew she has known for many summers.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because most of her twenty-five-person harvest crew would lose their jobs within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Government support for apprenticeships so her workers can learn to run the machines, fairer supermarket contracts so small growers can afford robots, and less government interference otherwise.
